title: Activity Before Experience: Spontaneous Retinal Waves

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: Which retinal neurons send their axons into the optic nerve?
cards.back: Ganglion cells, the output neurons of the retina.
cards.quote: Ganglion cells are the retina's output neurons; their axons make up the optic nerve.

cards.front: Activity generated by a neural circuit without sensory input is called {{c1::spontaneous activity}}.
cards.back: The developing retina produces it as waves.
cards.quote: Spontaneous activity is activity that circuits generate on their own, without being driven by sensory input.
cards.section: The problem: a rough first draft

cards.front: How does refinement change the rough retinal projections initially positioned by molecular cues?
cards.back: Overlapping projections separate into eye-specific territories, and broadly branching axons become focal. Activity refines a map whose rough order molecular cues already established.
cards.quote: Getting from overlap to separate territories, and from broad branches to focal ones, is called refinement.
cards.section: The problem: a rough first draft

cards.front: How can retinal activity distinguish neighbouring cells in one eye from a cell at the matching position in the other eye?
cards.back: Neighbours in one eye fire together in waves; the other eye fires on its own schedule. Their relative timing supplies information their similar molecular labels cannot.
cards.quote: The two neighbours fire together; the cell in the other eye fires on its own schedule.
cards.section: Why activity? Two neighbours look the same to a gradient

cards.front: Under Hebb's postulate, a connection strengthens when presynaptic firing repeatedly helps the {{c1::postsynaptic cell}} fire.
cards.back: Presynaptic firing alone is insufficient; it must contribute to firing the target.
cards.quote: repeatedly takes part in firing it, some growth or metabolic change makes A more effective at firing B.
cards.section: Hebb's rule, and the half he did not write

cards.front: Why does Hebbian strengthening alone fail to separate two active input populations onto a target neuron?
cards.back: Each population can strengthen whenever it helps fire the target. Segregation also needs competition that lets stronger inputs gain at the expense of rivals.
cards.quote: Hebb's rule as written only strengthens, so every active input grows and the cell stays binocular.
cards.section: Hebb's rule, and the half he did not write

cards.front: In a toy model, left- and right-eye inputs start at 5.5 and 4.5 strength units. Each gains 20 percent, then loses 1 unit. What are the final strengths and their difference?
cards.back: Left: 5.5 × 1.2 − 1 = 5.6 units. Right: 4.5 × 1.2 − 1 = 4.4 units. Difference: 5.6 − 4.4 = 1.2 units, up from 1.0 unit.
cards.quote: So the gap grows from 1.0 to 1.2 units in one round; the eye that is ahead gains more than it gives back.
cards.section: Hebb's rule, and the half he did not write

cards.front: Why does proportional rescaling after equal percentage growth fail to segregate eye inputs in the toy model?
cards.back: It preserves their strength ratio, so the initially stronger eye never increases its share. A fixed total alone does not guarantee segregation.
cards.quote: Only the last row segregates. Shrinking by the same fraction keeps the ratio.
cards.section: Hebb's rule, and the half he did not write

cards.front: In the equal-subtraction toy model, right-eye inputs begin slightly stronger than left-eye inputs. What happens after repeated rounds, and why?
cards.back: Right-eye inputs eventually win and left-eye inputs reach zero. Equal percentage growth followed by equal subtraction amplifies the initial advantage; the rule has no built-in preference for an eye.
cards.quote: Whichever eye starts ahead wins; exactly equal eyes stay equal, but any small difference grows
cards.section: Hebb's rule, and the half he did not write

cards.front: How do competition for a limited survival factor and competition for limited synaptic territory implement the same developmental principle?
cards.back: Both combine retention of successful cells or inputs with a limited shared resource. By the competition rule, success becomes relative: retaining more for one rival leaves less for another.
cards.quote: In both cases a shortage turns "keep what works" into "keep what works better than its rivals".
cards.section: Hebb's rule, and the half he did not write

cards.front: With glutamate and a co-agonist bound, sufficient depolarization permits NMDA receptor current by relieving {{c1::magnesium block}}.
cards.back: The pore conducts little current while the block remains.
cards.quote: the membrane is depolarized enough to relieve magnesium block of its pore.
cards.section: A detector for "together"

cards.front: How can an NMDA receptor link coincident synaptic input to a lasting synaptic change?
cards.back: Glutamate arriving during depolarization permits strong current when a co-agonist is bound. Calcium entry can trigger lasting synaptic changes.
cards.quote: It admits calcium, which can set off lasting changes in the synapse
cards.section: A detector for "together"

cards.front: Calcium imaging shows retinal activity waves propagating through the visual system of live neonatal mice before eye opening. What concern about isolated-retina recordings does this address?
cards.back: The waves are not merely an artefact of an isolated retina in a dish. Observing them in vivo does not establish their wiring function.
cards.quote: saw waves of retinal activity propagate through the visual system before the eyes opened, so the pattern is not an artefact of a dish.
cards.section: What the waves look like

cards.front: A retinal wave moves along the line joining two cells 60 micrometres apart at about 100 micrometres per second. Each bursts for 2 seconds. What fraction of the first burst overlaps the second?
cards.back: Lag = 60/100 = 0.6 seconds. Overlap = 2 − 0.6 = 1.4 seconds; overlapping fraction = 1.4/2 = 0.70, or about 70 percent.
cards.quote: Time apart is distance divided by speed. The overlap is the part of the 2-second burst left after that lag:
cards.section: What the waves look like

cards.front: At about 100 micrometres per second with 2-second bursts, what separation along a retinal wave's direction of travel leaves no burst overlap? Would this be a sharp boundary in a real retina?
cards.back: Separation = speed × burst length = 100 × 2 = about 200 micrometres. At that separation the lag equals the burst duration. Real correlations fade gradually because waves vary in direction and extent.
cards.quote: Along a wave's path, overlap runs out at wave speed times burst length, here 200 micrometres.
cards.section: What the waves look like

cards.front: Two neural populations generate bursts independently. A target receives one input from each. Does a burst in one population imply a coincident burst in the other, and why?
cards.back: No. Coincidence occurs only by chance because the populations have independent timing. Activity in both populations does not ensure correlated input to their shared target.
cards.quote: W's waves are not timed to this eye's at all;
cards.section: What the waves look like

cards.front: Why can a developing target infer retinal neighbourhood from repeated pairwise timing but not reliably from a single ganglion cell's firing time?
cards.back: Waves start in different places and travel in varying directions, changing absolute firing times. The stated timing rule instead uses the repeated coincidence of neighbours across waves to reflect proximity.
cards.quote: Only how closely two cells' firing matches, averaged over many waves, reflects how far apart they are.
cards.section: What the waves look like

cards.front: The dominant drivers of retinal waves progress from gap junctions to {{c1::acetylcholine}} to glutamate.
cards.back: The stages overlap; their boundaries are approximate.
cards.quote: The waves are not driven by one mechanism throughout development. The dominant driver changes in three stages,
cards.section: What makes a wave, briefly

cards.front: Which cells release the acetylcholine that drives stage II retinal waves, and which receptor class receives it?
cards.back: Starburst amacrine cells release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors.
cards.quote: waves require synaptic activation of nicotinic receptors, and that the only cholinergic cells present were the starburst amacrine cells.
cards.section: What makes a wave, briefly

cards.front: Which tool targets the direct intercellular coupling involved in stage I retinal waves?
cards.back: Gap junction blockers. Stage I also depends on nicotinic receptors, so its mechanism is not exclusively gap junctional.
cards.quote: Stage I waves, before birth, depend on gap junctions and also on nicotinic receptors;
cards.section: The stages in more detail

cards.front: Which receptor blockers remove or alter stage III retinal waves?
cards.back: Glutamate receptors; glutamate receptor blockers remove or alter these waves.
cards.quote: The dominant driver changes in three stages, best worked out in mice, rabbits and ferrets;
cards.section: What makes a wave, briefly

cards.front: Why does tetrodotoxin stop neuronal action potentials?
cards.back: It blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing the spikes they support.
cards.quote: tetrodotoxin (TTX), which blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and so stops action potentials (spikes),
cards.section: Block it: silence everything

cards.front: Fetal cats given tetrodotoxin in the brain retain overlapping eye projections in the LGN. Why does this establish a need for spikes without isolating competition between the eyes?
cards.back: The drug would be expected to reach both eyes' axons and LGN neurons. Global silencing shows a requirement for spikes but cannot isolate relative eye activity or the essential spike source.
cards.quote: So the experiment shows that spikes are needed, but cannot tell you whether the eyes compete by their activity,
cards.section: Block it: silence everything

cards.front: What distinguishes a permissive developmental signal from an instructive one?
cards.back: A permissive signal needs to be present for wiring to form; an instructive signal's pattern tells the wiring what to do.
cards.quote: A permissive signal only has to be present for the wiring to form; an instructive signal's pattern tells the wiring what to do.
cards.section: Block it: silence everything

cards.front: A developmental signal is necessary for normal wiring. Design a further test of whether it instructs the wiring, and state the informative outcome.
cards.back: Change where or when the signal is delivered and test whether the wiring changes accordingly. This uses the instructive-signal rule: pattern guides the outcome, whereas removing the signal tests necessity alone.
cards.quote: To show that a signal instructs, you change where or when it is delivered and see whether the outcome follows.
cards.section: Block it: silence everything

cards.front: In a young ferret, epibatidine disrupts waves in the right eye while the left eye retains normal waves. What happens to the two LGN projections, and why?
cards.back: The left-eye projection expands and the treated right-eye projection shrinks. Relative activity shifts shared territory through competition; the shift is graded rather than complete takeover.
cards.quote: the projection from the active retina expanded into territory that normally belongs to the other eye, and the treated eye's projection shrank.
cards.section: Tilt it: make the eyes unequal

cards.front: How can the nicotinic agonist epibatidine disrupt cholinergic retinal waves while the retina continues to fire?
cards.back: It is thought to persistently activate and desensitize nicotinic receptors, disrupting normal wave organization without eliminating all firing.
cards.quote: a nicotinic agonist thought to disrupt cholinergic waves by persistently activating and desensitizing the receptors (the treated retina keeps firing, without normal waves)
cards.section: Tilt it: make the eyes unequal

cards.front: Two input populations share limited target territory. Under a relative-activity model, correlated drive rises in one while its rival stays unchanged. What happens to territory, and why?
cards.back: The more active population gains territory at its rival's expense. The stated competition rule allocates a shared target according to relative activity, so the rival need not become less active to lose ground.
cards.quote: When one eye was made more active, its layer was larger even though the other eye was normal.
cards.section: Tilt it: make the eyes unequal

cards.front: Two competing input populations receive equal increases in correlated activity. Under a relative-activity model, what happens to their shares of target territory, and why?
cards.back: Their shares remain unchanged because neither gains a relative advantage. The model ties territory to the difference between competitors rather than total activity.
cards.quote: the eyes divide a shared target, so raising both equally gives neither more of it: territory follows the difference between the eyes, not the total.
cards.section: Tilt it: make the eyes unequal

cards.front: A drug changes spike count and burst timing together, and a developing map changes. Design a comparison that better isolates timing as the instructive variable.
cards.back: Compare populations with matched overall activity but different temporal patterns. If maps differ, this supports instruction by pattern. This follows the rule that changing a signal's pattern tests what information it carries.
cards.quote: these drugs change wave frequency and pattern as well as the number of spikes, so they do not say which feature of the activity counts.
cards.section: Tilt it: make the eyes unequal

cards.front: In the superior colliculus, what does a broad termination zone from neighbouring retinal ganglion cells indicate?
cards.back: A poorly sharpened retinotopic map. A small termination zone indicates a sharp map.
cards.quote: The zone is small if the map is sharp and broad if it is not.
cards.section: Disrupt the correlation, keep plenty of spikes

cards.front: In the reported beta2-knockout mouse study, early firing was abundant but uncorrelated. Would later glutamatergic waves and vision rescue refinement, and why?
cards.back: Not in this study: the zones remained broad. The result supports an early window for normally patterned activity; later correlated input did not repair the earlier failure to refine.
cards.quote: That points to an early window: in this study, correlated activity arriving later did not sharpen zones that had already stayed broad.
cards.section: Disrupt the correlation, keep plenty of spikes

cards.front: Why is it too strong to conclude that beta2-knockout mouse retinas never produce waves?
cards.back: Later laboratories recorded correlated but altered waves under some conditions. The defensible claim is loss of normal wave patterns, not universal absence of waves.
cards.quote: Later laboratories recorded correlated but altered waves in beta2 knockout retinas under some conditions, so the mutants lack normal waves rather than all waves.
cards.section: Disrupt the correlation, keep plenty of spikes

cards.front: A frog tectal lobe normally receives axons from one eye. When an extra eye also projects there, alternating eye-specific bands form. What does this show?
cards.back: Interactions between competing retinal inputs can produce stripes where none normally occur. The result alone does not identify the underlying molecular mechanism.
cards.quote: The two projections formed alternating bands, so interaction between the inputs created stripes where none normally exist.
cards.section: Add an eye: the three-eyed frog

cards.front: In a three-eyed tadpole, active APV removes tectal stripes while retinal axons still respond. What does this imply about NMDA receptors beyond the presence of axonal activity?
cards.back: Maintaining the stripes requires NMDA receptor activity in the frog tectum. Continuing retinal axon responses show that loss of all axonal activity is not needed for stripes to disappear.
cards.quote: The active form of APV desegregated the stripes, while the retinal axons still responded;
cards.section: Add an eye: the three-eyed frog

cards.front: In three-eyed tadpoles, inactive APV leaves tectal stripes normal and stripes return after active APV is removed. How do these controls strengthen the interpretation of active APV?
cards.back: The inactive form argues against an effect shared by both forms, and recovery shows reversible disruption. Combined with APV's receptor action, these controls support the rule that NMDA receptor activity maintains frog stripes.
cards.quote: the inactive form left them normal; NMDA itself sharpened their borders; and after APV was removed the stripes returned within two weeks.
cards.section: Add an eye: the three-eyed frog

cards.front: In the illustrative simulation, a target samples inputs across 300 micrometres while firing overlap extends about 200 micrometres. Would compact surviving patches show that the target became eye-dominated, and why?
cards.back: No. The model drops distant inputs and retains compact patches, but no cell becomes eye-dominated in this condition. Spatial refinement does not guarantee eye segregation; the outcome depends on the input geometry and competitive rule.
cards.quote: the rule drops the distant inputs, so each eye keeps a compact patch, but no cell becomes eye-dominated.
cards.section: Why Hebb needed a second half

cards.front: A beta2 knockout removes the subunit throughout the animal. Why does restoring beta2 only in retinal ganglion cells help interpret the map defect?
cards.back: It localizes the test to a retinal contribution rather than relying on a whole-animal deletion. The retinal restoration work keeps the retina central, without making the original knockout retina-specific.
cards.quote: A knockout removes the subunit everywhere, not only in the retina.
cards.section: The beta2 knockout, more carefully

cards.front: Why does preserved eye segregation after depletion of starburst amacrine cells in ferrets not settle whether correlated retinal activity instructs segregation?
cards.back: Enough correlated activity may remain to support segregation. Removing a cell population is not equivalent to demonstrating elimination of the relevant activity pattern.
cards.quote: Others argued that enough correlated activity remained in those retinas to do the job;
cards.section: Are the waves instructive? A long debate

cards.front: Does NMDA-dependent stripe maintenance in the frog establish that the same receptor separates eye inputs in the mammalian LGN? Reconcile the evidence.
cards.back: No. NMDA blockade did not prevent eye segregation in ferret LGN, although it disrupted later ON/OFF sublayers. The rule is system-specific: the frog tests NMDA-dependent maintenance; the mammalian eye-segregation detector remains unresolved.
cards.quote: In ferrets, an NMDA receptor blocker did not prevent the two eyes from segregating in the LGN
cards.section: NMDA receptors in the mammalian LGN
